title: Atypical Autoimmune Encephalitis: Diagnostic Challenges and Therapeutic Insights From a Case Series
summary: A case series of patients with atypical autoimmune encephalitis highlights diagnostic delays, heterogeneous presentations, and variable antibody testing results. The report emphasizes the importance of multimodal assessment, early empirical immunotherapy when clinical suspicion is high, and tailored escalation to second-line agents for refractory cases. It calls for standardized protocols and prospective studies to improve recognition and outcomes.
content:
A recent case series focused on atypical presentations of autoimmune encephalitis underscores persistent diagnostic challenges faced by clinicians. Patients in the series presented with a spectrum of neuropsychiatric and neurologic symptoms, including subacute cognitive decline, new-onset psychiatric manifestations, movement disorders, seizures, and fluctuating levels of consciousness. Many cases lacked classic serologic markers, complicating early confirmation.

Standard diagnostic workups frequently included brain MRI, EEG, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis, yet imaging and CSF findings were often nondiagnostic or showed only subtle abnormalities. Routine autoimmune antibody panels returned negative or inconclusive results in a significant subset of patients, prompting clinicians to rely heavily on clinical assessment and ancillary testing. The series emphasizes that negative antibody tests do not rule out an autoimmune etiology.

The authors report that delayed recognition led to postponed initiation of immunotherapy in several patients, with consequences for recovery trajectory. Empirical treatment with high-dose corticosteroids or intravenous immunoglobulin was commonly used when clinical suspicion was strong. In patients who failed to improve, escalation to plasmapheresis or steroid-sparing agents such as rituximab or cyclophosphamide produced variable but sometimes substantial clinical gains.

Management decisions were individualized, balancing the risks of immunosuppression against the potential for neurologic deterioration. Multidisciplinary collaboration among neurology, psychiatry, infectious disease, and immunology teams aided diagnostic clarification and treatment planning. Serial assessments, repeat antibody testing, and follow-up imaging were useful when initial studies were nondiagnostic, as delayed seroconversion or evolving imaging abnormalities were observed in some cases.

Outcomes varied across the series, with earlier treatment generally associated with better functional recovery. Some patients experienced prolonged rehabilitation needs, persistent cognitive deficits, or relapses requiring maintenance immunotherapy. The report highlights the need for clear criteria to identify patients who should receive early empirical therapy despite negative initial serology.

The case series concludes with practical recommendations: maintain a high index of suspicion for autoimmune encephalitis in atypical subacute presentations, use multimodal diagnostic approaches, consider early empirical immunotherapy when clinical probability is moderate to high, and plan for long-term follow-up and rehabilitation. The authors call for prospective studies and standardized diagnostic algorithms to reduce delays, better define antibody-negative syndromes, and optimize therapeutic strategies.

- New-onset psychiatric manifestations

- Imaging and CSF were often nondiagnostic or subtly abnormal

- Clinical assessment and ancillary testing played a central role

- Empirical therapies used:

  - Rituximab
  - Cyclophosphamide
- Strategies that aided care:
  - Multidisciplinary collaboration
  - Serial clinical assessments
  - Repeat antibody testing
  - Follow-up imaging

The case series concludes with practical recommendations:

- Plan for long-term follow-up and rehabilitation
